title: 1. What is Data Visualization
content:
Data visualization is all about turning data into pictures that help us understand it better. Instead of staring at rows of numbers or text, visualization uses charts, graphs, or other visual tools to make patterns and relationships easier to see. The main reason this works is because our eyes and brain are really good at processing visual information quickly and in parallel. When we look at a well-designed visualization, we can often grasp the big picture and spot details at the same time, which is much harder to do with raw data alone.

One important thing to understand is why we need humans involved in the process. Sometimes, computers can analyze data automatically and give us answers, but many problems are not that straightforward. Often, we don’t know exactly what questions to ask or what patterns to look for before we start. That’s where visualization shines—it helps people explore data, discover unexpected insights, and make decisions based on what they see. Visualization is also useful for communicating results to others, whether it’s in a scientific paper or a news article. It can even help developers improve automatic analysis tools by showing them what’s going on inside the data.

Vision is the best sense for this kind of work because it can handle a lot of information at once. Our eyes take in a wide view, and our brains process many visual elements simultaneously without us having to focus on each one individually. This is different from hearing, which is more sequential and slower to process, or touch, which can’t easily record and replay complex information. Because of this, visualizations let us see the whole dataset at once, making it easier to understand patterns and spot outliers.

It’s also important to show all the data, not just summaries like averages or correlations. Summaries can hide important details or unusual cases. A classic example is a set of datasets that all have the same basic statistics but look very different when graphed. This shows why looking at the full data visually is crucial to avoid missing something important.

When designing visualizations, we have to keep in mind some practical limits. Computers have limits on how fast they can process data and how much memory they have. Screens have limited pixels, so we have to balance showing enough information without making the display cluttered or confusing. At the same time, humans have limited attention and memory, so visualizations need to be clear and not overwhelming. Good design finds a balance between showing enough detail and keeping things simple enough to understand.

Finally, analyzing visualization methods helps us make better choices. There are many ways to show data, and not all of them work well for every task or dataset. By studying existing visualizations and understanding their strengths and weaknesses, we can create new designs that fit specific needs better. This kind of analysis helps us think clearly about what works and why, rather than just guessing.

In short, data visualization is a tool that helps people see and understand data by turning it into images. It works best when humans are involved to explore and interpret the data, especially when problems are complex or unclear. Our visual system is uniquely suited for this because it can process a lot of information quickly and in parallel. Showing all the data, not just summaries, is important to get the full picture. Designers must consider the limits of computers, screens, and human attention to create effective visualizations. And by analyzing how visualizations work, we can improve how we design them for different tasks.

title: 2. Nested Models
content:
When we talk about designing visualizations, it helps to think of the process as having several layers, each building on the one before it. Tamara Munzner’s Nested Model is a way to break down these layers so we can understand and improve how visualizations are created and evaluated. The model has four main levels, and each one asks a simple but important question that guides the design.

The first level is about the domain situation. This means understanding who the users are and what their real-world context looks like. It’s not just about knowing the data but about knowing the people who will use the visualization, what they want to achieve, and what tools they currently use. If you get this wrong, the whole visualization might miss the mark because it won’t address the actual needs of the users.

Once you understand the users and their context, the next step is to translate that into something a visualization can work with. This is called data and task abstraction. Here, you decide what data is important and what tasks the users want to perform with that data. For example, if you’re working with sales data, you might abstract it into categories like time periods or product types, and the tasks might be to find trends or compare sales between regions. This step is crucial because it turns messy, real-world information into a form that can be visually represented.

After you know what data and tasks you’re focusing on, the next level is about how to show that data and how users will interact with it. This involves choosing visual encoding idioms, which are the graphical elements like bars, lines, or colors that represent the data. It also involves interaction idioms, which are the ways users can manipulate the visualization, like zooming in, filtering, or selecting items. Picking the right visual and interaction methods is key to making the visualization clear and easy to use. If the visual design is confusing or the interaction is awkward, users won’t get the insights they need.

The last level is the algorithm, which is about how the visualization is actually built and runs behind the scenes. This includes the computational methods that process the data and render the visuals efficiently. If the algorithm is slow or uses too much memory, the visualization might be frustrating or impossible to use, no matter how good the design is.

These four levels are nested inside each other, meaning that problems at one level affect the others. For example, if you misunderstand the users’ needs at the domain level, you might choose the wrong data or tasks, which then leads to poor visual design and inefficient algorithms. On the other hand, issues found at the algorithm level, like slow performance, might make you rethink your visual encoding or even the data abstraction. So, designing a visualization is often an iterative process where you go back and forth between these levels to improve the overall system.

Validating a visualization is tricky because each level can fail in different ways. You might misunderstand the users, show the wrong data, design confusing visuals, or have slow code. Because of this, you need different methods to check each level. For example, to understand the domain, you might observe users in their real environment or interview them. To validate data and tasks, you compare your choices to alternatives and make sure they’re relevant. For visual encoding and interaction, lab studies can measure how quickly and accurately users perform tasks. For algorithms, you test system speed and memory use.

No single method can confirm that the whole visualization works well. Computational tests don’t guarantee the visuals are clear, and lab studies don’t prove the tasks are the right ones. That’s why combining methods from computer science, design, psychology, and anthropology is important.

Many research projects use parts of this model to guide their work. For example, some focus on algorithm efficiency, others on user studies, and some on qualitative analysis of the visuals. This shows how the nested model helps organize the complex process of visualization design and validation, making sure each part gets the attention it needs.

In short, the Nested Model helps us think clearly about visualization design by breaking it into four levels: understanding users, abstracting data and tasks, choosing how to show and interact with data, and implementing efficient algorithms. Each level depends on the others, and good design means carefully working through all of them, testing and refining as you go.

title: 3. Data Abstraction
content:
When we talk about data, it’s easy to think of it as just numbers or words, but data by itself doesn’t carry meaning until we understand the context behind it. For example, if I give you a list of numbers like 14, 2.6, 30, 30, 15, and 100001, you might wonder what they represent. Are these coordinates of points in space? Are they counts of something? Without knowing what these numbers relate to, they’re just symbols. The same goes for words like “Basil, 7, S, Pear.” This could be a shipment of produce arriving on the 7th day, or it could be a neighborhood named Basil Point with 7 inches of snow cleared by a company called Pear Creek. The point is, data needs meaning, or semantics, to be useful.

To make sense of data, we break it down into basic parts. One key idea is the difference between items and attributes. An item is a single entity you’re studying, like a patient, a car, or a city. Attributes are the properties or characteristics of those items, like a patient’s height or a car’s horsepower. So, if you think of a table listing people, each row is an item, and each column is an attribute describing something about that person. Besides items and attributes, data can also include links, which show relationships between items, like friendships on social media or interactions between proteins. Positions are another type, representing spatial locations, such as points on a map or pixels in an image. Grids are a way to organize data sampled regularly over space, like temperature readings across a region.

Data can be organized in different ways depending on what it represents. The simplest form is a flat table, where each row is an item and each column is an attribute. Sometimes data is more complex, like multidimensional tables that use multiple keys to index data, such as gene expression levels measured across many patients. Another common form is networks or graphs, where items are nodes connected by links or edges. Trees are a special kind of graph without cycles, often with a root node. Spatial fields are data associated with cells in space, like temperature or wind velocity measured over an area. These can be scalars (single values), vectors (values with direction), or tensors (more complex data). Geometry refers to the shape and spatial properties of items, like points, lines, or volumes, and this is where visualization overlaps with computer graphics.

When grouping data, we often talk about sets, lists, or clusters. Sets are collections of unique items without order, lists are ordered and can have duplicates, and clusters are groups of similar items. Understanding how data is grouped helps in organizing and analyzing it.

Attributes themselves come in different types based on the kind of values they hold. Categorical attributes represent categories without any order, like blood types. Ordinal attributes have a meaningful order but no consistent difference between values, like rankings. Quantitative attributes have meaningful magnitudes and support arithmetic operations, like height or temperature. Knowing the attribute type is important because it affects how we analyze and visualize the data.

Data abstraction is the process of taking raw, domain-specific data and turning it into a form that can be used for visualization. This involves translating the specific language of the data into a more general form, identifying what kind of dataset it is, classifying attribute types, and understanding the size or cardinality of the data. For example, how many items are there? How many unique values does each attribute have? Sometimes, data needs to be transformed or simplified based on the task at hand, like grouping temperatures into categories such as hot, warm, or cold.

It’s also important to distinguish between data models and conceptual models. A data model is a mathematical or programming abstraction, like a list of numbers or strings. A conceptual model is how we understand what the data means in the real world, which helps us reason about it and decide how to use it. For example, a list of floating-point numbers might represent temperature readings. Depending on the task, we might treat these numbers differently: as continuous values for weather forecasting, as ordered categories for deciding if bath water is warm enough, or as simple categories like above or below freezing for deciding whether to leave the house.

Sometimes, we create new attributes from existing data, called derived attributes. These can be simple conversions, like changing units, or more complex calculations. For example, in network analysis, the Strahler number is a derived attribute that measures the importance of nodes in a tree or network. By calculating this number, we can focus on the most important parts of a large network, making it easier to visualize and understand.

In summary, understanding data abstraction means recognizing what data represents, how it’s structured, and how to transform it into forms that make sense for visualization. This involves knowing the types of data and attributes, the organization of datasets, and the difference between raw data and the meaning we assign to it. By doing this carefully, we ensure that visualizations are meaningful and help us make better decisions based on the data.

title: 4. Task Abstraction
content:
When we talk about designing visualizations, one of the key steps is something called task abstraction. This is basically about taking the specific questions and problems people have in a particular area—like healthcare, finance, or social media—and turning those into more general tasks that help us figure out what kind of visualization tools to build. The idea is to move from the detailed, sometimes complicated language of a specific field to a simpler, more universal way of describing what users want to do with their data. This makes it easier to design visualizations that work well for different kinds of users and problems.

To start, we need to understand the domain, which means getting a clear picture of who the users are, what their goals and questions are, and what kind of data they have. This is important because every domain is different, and the questions people ask can vary a lot. But once we have that understanding, the next step is to break down those specific questions into simpler, more abstract tasks. This involves two things: figuring out the general types of tasks users want to perform, and understanding the kinds of data that support those tasks. By doing this, we create a bridge between the real-world problems and the design of visualization tools.

At the core of task abstraction are two concepts: actions and targets. Actions are what users want to do with the data, and targets are the things they want to act on. For example, a user might want to discover the distribution of data, compare trends, or locate outliers. Each of these is a pair of an action and a target. These pairs give us a kind of vocabulary to describe user tasks in a way that doesn’t depend on the specific domain. This helps us think about visualization design in a more general way.

Designing a visualization system is an iterative process. First, we characterize the domain by understanding the users, their questions, and their data. Then, we translate those domain-specific tasks into abstract tasks. After that, we identify or create visualization techniques that support those tasks. We also map the domain-specific data into more general data abstractions. Finally, we select or develop algorithms that can process the data to support the tasks. This process often requires going back and forth between understanding the domain and refining the abstractions, because sometimes realizing what tasks users want to do leads us to change how we represent the data, or vice versa.

When we look more closely at the actions users perform, we can group them into three main types: analyze, search, and query. Analyzing means consuming data to gain insights. This can be split into discovering new information, which is more exploratory, and presenting known information, which is more about explaining. There are also other analysis actions like enjoying data casually or producing new data through annotation or derivation. Searching depends on what the user already knows. Sometimes they look up a known item, like a word in a dictionary. Other times they locate something when they know what it looks like but not exactly where it is, or they browse without a specific target, or explore more freely. Querying focuses on how much of the data the user wants to consider—whether they want to identify a single item, compare a few items, or summarize the whole dataset.

Targets are the things users want to act on. These can be individual data points, groups of data, patterns, trends, outliers, or structures like networks. When abstracting tasks, it’s important to remove domain-specific jargon and express targets in general terms. For example, instead of saying “genes” in biology, we might say “nodes” or “entities” in a network. The relationship between tasks and data is important because understanding the targets helps us decide how to represent the data, and sometimes the way the data is represented influences how we define the tasks.

Because task abstraction and data abstraction are closely connected, we often need to go through several rounds of refinement. We start with an initial understanding of the data and tasks, then create abstractions. As we design, we might realize the data needs to be transformed or represented differently to support the tasks better. This leads us to revise both the data and task abstractions until we have a clear and workable set of tasks and data types that guide the visualization design.

In summary, task abstraction is about translating complex, domain-specific problems into general tasks that help us design better visualizations. By focusing on what users want to do (actions) and what they want to do it to (targets), and by iterating between understanding the domain and refining abstractions, we can create visualization tools that are more useful and adaptable across different fields.

title: 5. Marks and Channels
content:
When we talk about visualizing data, one of the most important ideas to understand is how we turn raw information into something people can see and understand quickly. This process is called visual encoding, and it relies on two key concepts: marks and channels. Marks are the basic shapes or elements you see in a visualization, like dots, lines, or areas. Channels are the ways we change the appearance of those marks to show different pieces of information, such as changing their color, size, or position.

Think of marks as the building blocks. For example, a point might represent a single data item, a line might show a connection between two items, and an area could represent a group or category. Each type of mark has its own characteristics and limitations. Points are flexible because they don’t have a fixed size, so you can change their size or shape to show extra data. Lines have one dimension fixed by the data they represent, but you can still change their width or color. Areas have two fixed dimensions, so you can’t use size or shape to encode more data without causing confusion.

Channels are what make marks meaningful. They control how marks look based on the data attributes. For example, you might use color to show categories, size to show quantity, or position to show value. Different channels are better suited for different types of data. Position is great for showing precise numbers because people can judge spatial differences accurately. Color hue works well for categories because it helps us distinguish groups. Sometimes, the same data is encoded using multiple channels at once, like both color and size, to make the message stronger, but this uses up more visual resources.

Not all channels are equally effective. Some allow us to see differences very clearly, while others are harder to interpret. Length and position are among the most accurate channels because our eyes are good at judging distances and sizes. Color and shape are less precise but useful for grouping or categorizing data. The number of distinct steps or levels we can perceive in a channel is called discriminability. For example, line width can only show a few different levels before it becomes hard to tell them apart.

Another important idea is separability, which means how well we can perceive one channel independently of others. Sometimes, when multiple channels are combined, they interfere with each other, making it harder to understand the data. Popout is a phenomenon where certain visual features make an item stand out immediately, like a red dot among blue dots. This happens because our visual system processes some channels in parallel, allowing us to spot differences quickly.

How accurately we perceive these channels depends on several factors. Alignment is one of them—when marks are aligned on a common scale, it’s easier to compare them. The presence of many other marks, called distractors, can make it harder to judge differences. Distance between marks and whether they share a common scale also affect perception. Our visual system mostly makes relative judgments, meaning we compare things to their surroundings rather than judging absolute values. This is why having a shared frame or scale improves accuracy.

Color and brightness are special cases. Our perception of brightness depends on the contrast with surrounding areas, which is why some optical illusions trick us. Similarly, our brain maintains color constancy, so we see colors as stable even under different lighting conditions. This helps us recognize objects but can make precise color encoding tricky.

In summary, marks and channels are the foundation of visual encoding. Marks are the shapes that represent data, and channels are the visual properties that change to show different data attributes. Choosing the right combination depends on the type of data and how well people can perceive differences. Position and length are the most accurate channels for quantitative data, while color and shape work well for categories. Understanding these concepts helps us design visualizations that communicate data clearly and effectively.

title: 6. Perception
content:
Perception is how our brain makes sense of the world around us, especially through what we see. It’s not just about the eyes capturing images but about the brain actively interpreting and filtering information to focus on what matters. This process involves different ways of thinking that work together to help us understand and respond to our environment.

One way to understand how our brain processes information is through the idea of two systems of thinking. The first, often called System 1, is fast, automatic, and unconscious. It handles most of our thinking—about 98%—without us even realizing it. This system quickly assesses situations, recognizes faces, or reacts to things without effort or deliberate thought. It’s like the brain’s autopilot, making snap judgments based on what it immediately sees. The second system, System 2, is slower, conscious, and deliberate. It’s the part of our mind that steps in when we need to think carefully, solve problems, or make decisions. This system requires effort and self-awareness and only accounts for a small portion of our thinking, but it’s essential for reasoning and controlling impulses.

When it comes to vision, our eyes don’t take in a perfect, continuous picture like a camera. Instead, they sample the environment several times per second, and the brain pieces these snapshots together to form what we “see.” This means what we perceive depends not only on what’s actually there but also on what we expect to see and where we focus our attention. In other words, our brain fills in gaps based on past experience and current goals. Because our visual working memory is limited to holding only a few simple shapes at once, we can’t process every detail in a scene all at once.

Selective attention plays a big role in perception. It means we only notice what our mind focuses on, and everything else tends to fade into the background. This is why people can miss obvious things when they’re concentrating on something else, like in the famous basketball passing test where viewers don’t see a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. Other experiments show that even when talking to someone, people might not notice if that person is swapped with someone else during a brief interruption. These examples highlight that our perception is limited by what we pay attention to.

Color and depth perception are also influenced by context. The colors we see can change depending on shadows or the type of light shining on an object. For example, an object might look different under sunlight compared to indoor lighting because our brain adjusts how it interprets color. Depth perception helps us judge distances and see the world in three dimensions, relying on cues like size, shadows, and motion to create a sense of space.

When we look at visual information, our brain doesn’t process everything equally. According to research, we are especially sensitive to contrast and changes in what we see, and we tend to notice things that are familiar or that we expect. Our short-term visual memory is limited, so we can only hold a small amount of visual information at a time.

Perception happens in two stages. The first is pre-attentive perception, which is an immediate, automatic reaction to visual features like color, shape, or movement. This happens without conscious effort and helps us quickly spot important details. The second stage is post-attentive perception, which is slower and requires conscious effort. This is when we search for patterns or interpret complex information, often needing to think about what we see.

Our brain also uses certain principles to organize what we see into groups or patterns, known as Gestalt principles. For example, elements that look similar or are close together tend to be seen as part of the same group. If objects move in the same direction or are connected by lines, we naturally group them together. These principles help us make sense of complex visuals quickly.

Certain visual features stand out instantly to us without effort. These include differences in color brightness, shape, size, position, and movement. Designers and communicators use these features to make information easier to understand at a glance.

In summary, perception is an active process where our brain filters and interprets visual information using both fast, automatic thinking and slower, deliberate thought. Our eyes provide snapshots that the brain assembles, but what we actually see depends heavily on where we focus our attention. Because our memory and attention are limited, we only perceive a small part of what’s around us at any moment. Understanding how perception works helps us better interpret the world and design visuals that communicate clearly.

title: 7. Interactive Views
content:
Interactive views are a key part of modern data visualization that let users actively explore and understand data by changing what they see and how they see it. Instead of just looking at a static chart, you can interact with the visualization to filter data, reorder elements, or switch between different ways of showing the information. This kind of interaction means the view changes over time, which helps you discover patterns or details that might be hidden in a fixed image.

One common way to interact is by manipulating the visual encoding, which means changing how the data is represented visually. For example, you might switch from a bar chart to a line chart or adjust parameters like filters or thresholds to focus on specific parts of the data. Controls like sliders, buttons, and dropdown menus make these changes easy to do. They are usually labeled clearly so you know what they do, but they do take up space on the screen, so designers have to balance usability with keeping the view uncluttered.

Rearranging data is another useful interaction. You might reorder bars in a chart to highlight the highest or lowest values or sort a table by different columns to find correlations. Changing how elements are aligned, like switching between stacked and grouped bars, can also help you compare data more effectively. Animated transitions are often used to make these changes smooth, so you can follow how the data shifts without losing track of what you’re looking at. This is better than sudden jumps because it helps your brain stay oriented.

When designing interactive views, it’s important to think about the device people will use. On desktops, you have a mouse and keyboard, which support hovering and multiple clicks. On mobile devices, you only have taps and gestures, and no hover, so the interaction has to be simpler and more direct. New technologies like eye tracking or gesture sensors are emerging, but they come with their own challenges and aren’t widely used yet.

Selection and highlighting are basic but powerful interaction techniques. Selection means choosing one or more data points to focus on, and it can be done by clicking or tapping. Highlighting gives visual feedback on what’s selected, often by changing color, adding outlines, or adjusting size. This helps you see which items are important without changing the data itself. Sometimes motion is used to draw attention, but it can be distracting if overdone.

Navigation in interactive views means changing what part of the data you see and how you see it. This is often described using a camera metaphor: you can pan or scroll to move around, zoom in or out to see more or less detail, and in 3D views, rotate to look from different angles. Scrolling through a page to change the visualization, called scrollytelling, is common on the web because it feels natural, but it can sometimes behave unexpectedly or limit direct control.

Navigation can be unconstrained, where you move freely, or constrained, where the system guides you to focus on relevant parts of the data, often with smooth animated transitions. Constrained navigation helps prevent getting lost or overshooting your target.

When dealing with complex data, it’s often better to use multiple coordinated views instead of one big visualization. These views can show different aspects of the same data, and selections in one view highlight related data in others. This linking, sometimes called brushing and linking, helps you understand relationships across different views. For example, you might have an overview map and a detailed chart, and selecting a region on the map highlights the corresponding data in the chart.

Multiple views can be arranged side by side, called juxtaposition, or shown as small multiples, which are many small charts each showing a slice of the data. Juxtaposition uses more screen space but makes it easier to compare data because you can look back and forth instead of remembering what you saw before. Animated transitions can also show changes over time or between conditions, but they can be hard to follow if there are too many changes or frames.

Partitioning data means dividing it into groups or regions to make patterns easier to see. You might split data by categories like age or location, and then show each group separately or layered on top of each other. Layering means putting different sets of data in the same view but using different colors or styles to tell them apart. This works well for maps, where you might show roads on top of land areas, but it’s best to keep the number of layers small to avoid clutter.

Interaction has many benefits. It makes visualizations flexible and powerful, supports exploration by letting you change views as you go, and helps you switch between different tasks easily. Animated transitions help keep you oriented when things change. But interaction also has downsides. It takes time and mental effort, controls can clutter the screen or be hard to find, and users don’t always interact the way designers expect. For example, many people don’t use interactive features beyond simple scrolling.

Overall, interactive views turn data visualization from a static picture into a dynamic tool for discovery. They let you explore data in ways that static charts can’t, but they require careful design to make sure the interaction is clear, useful, and not overwhelming. When done well, they help you understand complex data more deeply and quickly.

title: 8. Visualization Design Principles
content:
When we talk about designing effective visualizations, the main goal is to present data in a way that makes it easy to understand and interpret. The foundation of good visualization comes from focusing on the data itself, not on unnecessary decorations or flashy effects that don’t add meaning. Edward Tufte, a key figure in this field, emphasized that the best visualizations show the data clearly and honestly, without clutter or distortion.

One of the most important ideas he introduced is the concept of the data-ink ratio. This means that most of what you see in a graph or chart should be directly related to the data. Any extra lines, colors, or shapes that don’t help explain the data should be removed. For example, instead of adding lots of gridlines or 3D effects, a simple, clean chart with clear labels is usually more effective. The goal is to use the minimum amount of ink or pixels needed to show the data clearly.

Along with that, it’s important to use space efficiently by increasing data density. This means showing as much relevant data as possible in a limited area without making the visualization confusing. Techniques like small multiples, which are a series of small charts showing different parts of the data, or sparklines, which are tiny line charts embedded in text, help pack more information into a small space. But it’s a balance—too much data can overwhelm the viewer, so clarity should never be sacrificed.

Context is another key part of good visualization. Data on its own can be hard to interpret, so providing comparisons or benchmarks helps people understand what the numbers really mean. For example, showing how current sales compare to last year’s or including a target line in a chart gives viewers a frame of reference to judge the data.

Accuracy and honesty in visualizations are crucial. The way data is shown should match the actual numbers without exaggeration or distortion. For instance, if a bar chart’s scale starts at a number other than zero, it can make differences look bigger than they really are. Tufte introduced the idea of a “lie factor” to measure how much a graphic distorts the data. A good visualization keeps this factor close to one, meaning the visual changes reflect the real changes in the data. Clear labeling and citing data sources also help maintain trust and transparency.

In today’s world, interactive visualizations are becoming more common. These allow users to explore the data themselves by zooming in, filtering, or drilling down into details. This kind of interaction helps people find insights that a static image might not reveal. For example, a dashboard where you can select different time periods or categories lets you tailor the view to your specific questions.

Accessibility is another important consideration. Visualizations should be designed so that everyone can understand them, including people with color blindness or other visual impairments. This means using color schemes that are distinguishable by all and providing alternative text descriptions for images. Being mindful of these factors makes your work more inclusive and effective.

When it comes to using 3D in visualizations, it’s usually best to be cautious. While 3D can look impressive, it often causes problems like perspective distortion, where objects farther away appear smaller, or occlusion, where parts of the data hide behind others. These issues can make it harder to read and interpret the data accurately. For most types of data, especially abstract or time-based data, 2D visualizations are clearer and easier to understand. 3D is best reserved for cases where the data truly exists in three dimensions, like spatial or shape data, and even then, it should be used carefully.

Another important point is how our brains process visual information. We are better at comparing things when we can see them side-by-side rather than having to remember what we saw earlier. This means that showing multiple small charts next to each other is often more effective than using animation to show changes over time. Animations can be useful for storytelling or showing transitions, but they are less helpful when you need to analyze many changes at once.

While immersive technologies like virtual reality are exciting, they don’t always add value for data visualization. High-resolution displays that show more detail are usually more helpful than immersion, especially for abstract data. Desktop environments tend to work better for most analysis tasks because they integrate well with other tools and workflows.

A useful approach to interactive visualization design is the mantra “overview first, zoom and filter, details on demand.” This means starting with a summary view of the data, allowing users to zoom into areas they’re interested in, and providing detailed information only when requested. This helps manage complexity and keeps the visualization from becoming overwhelming.

Finally, it’s important to focus on function before form. The purpose of the visualization—what you want to communicate—should come first. Once the function is clear and the data is accurately represented, you can improve the visual appeal. Good design helps guide the viewer’s eye and makes the information easier to digest, but it should never come at the expense of clarity or accuracy. If you’re not confident in your design skills, working with a graphic designer can help make your visualizations both useful and attractive.

In summary, effective visualization is about showing data clearly, honestly, and efficiently. It’s about helping people understand the story behind the numbers without distractions or distortions. By following these principles, you can create visualizations that are not only informative but also trustworthy and accessible.

title: 9. Visualizations for Tabular Data
content:
When we talk about visualizing tabular data, we’re dealing with information organized in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet. The goal is to turn those numbers and categories into pictures that help us see patterns, relationships, or trends more easily than just scanning raw data. At the heart of this are two ideas: keys and values. Keys are the unique identifiers or categories that help us find or group data points, like product names or dates. Values are the numbers or measurements associated with those keys, like sales figures or temperatures. Sometimes there’s just one key, sometimes multiple, and that affects how we visualize the data.

One of the simplest and most common visualizations is the scatterplot. It shows the relationship between two numerical variables by plotting points on a grid, where each point’s position corresponds to the values of those variables. Scatterplots are great for spotting trends, clusters, or outliers. You can add more information by changing the color, size, or shape of the points, but you have to be careful with size because our eyes perceive area differently than length. Sometimes, connecting the points with lines creates a connected scatterplot, which is useful for showing how data changes over time, though it can sometimes make it harder to see the exact correlation.

Bar charts are another staple. They work well when you have one categorical key and one numerical value. Each bar’s length represents the value, making it easy to compare categories. Bars are usually arranged side by side and can be ordered alphabetically or by size. When you add another categorical key, you get stacked bar charts, where each bar is divided into colored segments representing subcategories. This helps show how parts make up a whole, but it can get cluttered if there are too many segments or bars. Streamgraphs are a variation of stacked charts that emphasize smooth, flowing layers over time, often used to show things like movie box office trends.

Line charts and dot charts are similar but focus on ordered keys, like time. They connect points with lines to highlight trends or changes. It’s important to use line charts only when the key is ordered because lines imply continuity. Using lines for purely categorical data can mislead people into seeing trends that aren’t there. Sometimes, people use dual-axis line charts to compare two variables with different scales, but these can be confusing or misleading if not done carefully.

There are also charts designed to show changes between two points, like slopegraphs, which connect two values for each item with a line to highlight increases or decreases. Gantt charts are useful for showing tasks or events over time, with bars representing durations and start times, helping to visualize overlaps and dependencies.

Heatmaps take a different approach by arranging two categorical keys along the rows and columns of a grid, coloring each cell based on a numerical value. This makes it easy to spot clusters or unusual values across many categories. Cluster heatmaps add another layer by grouping similar rows and columns together, often shown with tree diagrams, to help understand the structure in the data.

Radial and circular charts, like radial bar charts, star plots, radar plots, pie charts, and coxcomb charts, arrange data around a circle. While they can look interesting, they often make it harder to accurately compare values because our eyes are better at judging length along straight lines than angles or areas in circles. Pie charts, for example, are okay for showing a few parts of a whole but become confusing with many categories. Radar plots are generally discouraged unless the data is naturally cyclic.

When dealing with many variables, scatterplot matrices show all pairwise scatterplots in a grid, helping to explore relationships between multiple numerical attributes. Parallel coordinates take a different approach by lining up all variables as parallel axes and drawing each data point as a line crossing these axes. This can reveal patterns across many dimensions but requires careful ordering of axes and some experience to interpret.

Throughout all these visualizations, it’s important to label axes clearly and avoid tricks like cropping the y-axis, which can distort how changes appear. Choosing the right chart depends on the data type and what you want to learn from it. Some charts work better for comparing categories, others for showing trends over time, and some for exploring complex relationships. Understanding the strengths and limitations of each helps you pick the best way to tell the story your data holds.

title: 10. Network and Spatial
content:
When we talk about network and spatial visualizations, we're dealing with two types of data that help us understand relationships and locations. Networks are all about connections—how things relate to each other—while spatial data focuses on where things are in physical or geographic space. Both types of data are common in many fields, from social media analysis to mapping disease outbreaks, and visualizing them effectively helps us see patterns and make sense of complex information.

Network data consists of nodes, which are the individual items, and links, which are the connections between those items. Think of nodes as people in a social network and links as friendships. Sometimes, networks form special structures called trees, where each node has one parent and there are no loops. This hierarchical structure is common in things like organizational charts or file systems.

When working with networks, there are two main kinds of tasks. One is topology-based, which means focusing on the structure of the network itself—finding paths between nodes, identifying neighbors, measuring how central or important a node is, or spotting clusters of closely connected nodes. The other is attribute-based, which looks at the properties of nodes or links, like whether a person has a pet or what type of relationship two nodes share. Often, we combine these tasks, such as finding friends-of-friends who like cats, which involves both the network structure and node attributes.

To visualize networks, the most common method is the node-link diagram. Here, nodes are shown as points and links as lines connecting them. This is intuitive because it directly shows connections, but it can get messy when there are many nodes or links. Good layouts try to reduce line crossings and node overlaps, keep connected nodes close, and use space efficiently. However, these goals often conflict, so algorithms try to find a balance.

One popular approach is force-directed placement, which imagines links as springs pulling connected nodes together and nodes as magnets pushing each other apart. The algorithm starts with nodes placed randomly and then moves them around until the forces balance out. This usually produces a reasonable layout for small or sparse networks, making clusters visible and keeping edge lengths fairly uniform. But it can be slow and unpredictable for very large networks.

Other node-link layouts include circular layouts, where nodes are arranged around a circle or along a line. These can reduce clutter if the order of nodes is chosen carefully, but the ordering itself can be tricky to determine. Another way to represent networks is with adjacency matrices, which use a grid where rows and columns represent nodes, and each cell shows whether a link exists between those nodes. This method scales better for large networks and avoids the problem of crossing lines, but it’s less intuitive for tracing paths.

Sometimes, hybrid visualizations combine node-link diagrams and adjacency matrices to get the best of both worlds. For example, NodeTrix uses matrices to show dense clusters and node-link diagrams for sparser parts of the network.

Trees, as a special kind of network, are often visualized differently to highlight their hierarchical nature. Node-link trees use layouts that arrange nodes neatly to avoid overlap, either in straight lines or radially around a center point. Radial layouts show depth by distance from the center and group siblings by angle, making it easier to understand the structure. Another approach is treemaps, which use nested rectangles sized according to a quantitative attribute, like file sizes in a folder. These are good for showing how a total quantity is divided among parts.

There are also implicit tree layouts like sunburst and icicle plots, which show hierarchy through position rather than explicit links. Sunbursts use a circular layout, while icicle plots use a rectangular one. These methods emphasize depth and sibling order but may hide some connection details.

Spatial data, on the other hand, always includes location information. This data is visualized to understand spatial relationships, such as where events happen or how something is distributed geographically. Common visualizations include choropleth maps, symbol maps, cartograms, and dot density maps.

Choropleth maps color geographic regions based on a data attribute, like population density or average income. They use the actual shapes of regions, which helps understand spatial relationships. However, they can be misleading if the data isn’t normalized properly. For example, showing total population without adjusting for area or density can make large but sparsely populated regions look more important than they really are. It’s best to use choropleth maps when the main goal is to understand spatial patterns and to show only one variable at a time.

Symbol maps place symbols like circles on specific locations, with size or color representing data values. These can help avoid the problem of region size bias in choropleth maps but can suffer from overlapping symbols, especially in dense areas. Complex symbols or glyphs can show multiple variables but may require explanation.

Cartograms distort the size of geographic regions to reflect data values, making large differences more obvious. Contiguous cartograms keep regions connected but change their shapes, while grid cartograms use uniform shapes arranged roughly in the original spatial order. Cartograms can be engaging but are harder to interpret because the shapes are distorted, so they work best when users are familiar with the original geography.

Dot density maps use dots to represent counts of a phenomenon, placing them within regions to show distribution and clustering. Each dot stands for a fixed number of items, and color can add another layer of information. These maps avoid some problems of choropleths but make it hard to extract exact quantities and can be slow to render if there are many dots.

In summary, network and spatial visualizations each have their own challenges and techniques. Networks focus on connections and structure, visualized through node-link diagrams, adjacency matrices, and trees, while spatial data relies on geographic position, visualized through maps like choropleths, symbol maps, cartograms, and dot density maps. Choosing the right visualization depends on the data, the questions you want to answer, and the size and complexity of the dataset. Understanding these basics helps you create clear and useful visualizations that reveal meaningful insights.

title: 11. Evaluation of Data Visualizations
content:
Data visualization is a tool we use to make sense of complex information by turning it into images like charts and graphs. But not every visualization does a good job. Some can confuse or mislead, while others clearly show what’s important. So, it’s useful to have a way to evaluate how well a visualization works. One practical approach is to use a checklist that looks at different parts of a graph or chart to see if it meets certain guidelines. For example, the title should be short but descriptive, placed where people naturally look first, usually the upper left corner. Subtitles and annotations can help explain or highlight key points. Text should be easy to read, with a clear hierarchy—titles bigger than labels, labels bigger than axis text—and generally horizontal so it’s easier to scan. Data labels should be placed close to the data itself rather than in a separate legend, which forces the viewer to look back and forth and interrupts understanding. Labels should also be used sparingly to avoid clutter.

The way the graph is arranged matters too. The proportions shown should accurately reflect the data, like bars starting at zero so the size matches the value. Data should be ordered logically, whether by time, size, or category, to help the viewer follow the story. Axis intervals should be evenly spaced, and the graph should avoid unnecessary 3D effects or decorations that don’t add meaning. Color use is important as well. Colors should be chosen intentionally, not just default settings, and should help highlight the most important parts of the data. They should also be readable for people with colorblindness and still make sense if printed in black and white. Text should contrast well with the background for easy reading.

Lines like gridlines and borders can add noise if overused, so they should be minimal and muted if present. Usually, a graph should have just one horizontal and one vertical axis to keep things simple. Overall, a good visualization should clearly highlight the main message or finding, use the right type of graph for the data, and present information with the right level of detail for the audience. When all these elements work together, the viewer can understand and remember the information better.

Beyond these practical tips, it’s helpful to think about what makes visualization valuable in the first place. Visualization is a way to turn data into images that help people gain knowledge. But this process depends on the data itself, the way the visualization is made, and the person looking at it. Someone with more background knowledge or better visual skills might get more out of the same image than someone else. Also, people often interact with visualizations, changing settings or exploring different views, which can help them learn more but also adds complexity.

To decide if a visualization method is worth using, we can think about the costs and benefits. Costs include the time and money spent developing the method, learning how to use it, preparing data, and exploring the visualization. Benefits come from the knowledge gained and how useful that knowledge is for making decisions. A good visualization method is one that many people use regularly because it helps them get valuable insights without too much effort or expense.

Measuring how much knowledge a visualization provides is tricky. We can’t directly see how much insight someone gains or how valuable it is. One way to think about it is to consider what actions the user takes after seeing the visualization. For example, does it help a doctor decide on a treatment, or help a manager make a business decision? If a visualization doesn’t lead to any clear action or better understanding, its value is questionable.

It’s also important to remember that visualization isn’t always the best way to get information. Sometimes automated methods can extract what we need more efficiently. Visualization is most useful when those methods don’t exist or can’t capture the full picture. Combining automated analysis with visualization can be powerful.

One big challenge is that new visualization methods often have high initial costs for users. People have to learn new tools, convert their data, and figure out if the method really helps. This can be a big barrier, especially if existing simpler tools already do an okay job. That’s why many users stick with basic visualization options built into software they already use.

Another thing to keep in mind is that visualization is subjective. Different people might see different things in the same image depending on their knowledge and how the visualization was made. Sometimes, a visualization might even be misleading if the data is processed or displayed incorrectly. For example, smoothing or interpolating data can create patterns that aren’t really there. That’s why expert judgment and validation are important.

Interaction with visualizations is generally seen as a good thing because it lets users explore data more deeply. But it can also increase the time and effort needed, and sometimes users might tweak settings to make the data look a certain way, which can be misleading. Good visualization tools should have sensible default settings that give useful views without much effort.

Looking at real examples helps understand these ideas. Texture-based flow visualization, which shows fluid movement using detailed textures, was developed decades ago and works well technically. But it’s not widely used in industry because the user base is small, the benefits over simpler methods are unclear, and the costs to learn and use it are high. On the other hand, cushion treemaps, which visualize hierarchical data like the contents of a hard drive, have been very successful. A tool called SequoiaView uses this method and has been downloaded hundreds of thousands of times. It meets a clear user need, is easy to use, and has few alternatives, so it scores high on value.

Visualization is used both for exploring unknown data and for presenting known results. While researchers often focus on exploration, presentation is just as important. Visualizations help communicate findings to others, whether in science, business, or marketing. For presentations, the audience is usually large and less familiar with the topic, so visualization can have a big impact.

When thinking about visualization, it helps to consider three perspectives. First, as a technology, visualization should be judged by how useful and efficient it is. Many ideas don’t make it into widespread use because of high costs or lack of clear benefits. Bridging the gap between research and practical use requires effort and sometimes commercial support. Second, visualization can be seen as an art form, valued for its beauty and creativity even if it’s not always practical. Third, visualization is a scientific discipline that needs theories, models, and empirical studies to understand what works and why. Developing taxonomies of methods, studying how people perceive visualizations, and creating guidelines are all part of this.

In the end, the value of visualization depends on what you want to achieve. If it helps people understand data better and make better decisions without too much cost, it’s valuable. If it’s just pretty but confusing, or too hard to use, it’s less so. Keeping these ideas in mind can help create visualizations that truly make a difference.
